hook_text: A pot of porridge left alone for three days starts to bubble, froth and smell different. Nobody added anything. What happened?
clip_script: A clay pot of umqombothi stands in a warm corner. Sprouted sorghum and maize porridge, left alone. After a day it starts to bubble. Froth forms. It smells sour, then a little like beer. Nobody added anything. Living yeasts did it. They ate the sugar from the sprouted grain and, with no oxygen around, turned it into alcohol and carbon dioxide. That is fermentation, a chemical reaction run by micro-organisms, and families in South Africa have controlled it for generations, judging by smell and taste exactly when it is ready. Leave milk in a calabash and other bacteria turn its sugar into lactic acid, making thick sour amasi that keeps for days without a fridge. Fifteen hundred years ago, smelters here were pulling oxygen out of iron ore in clay furnaces with goatskin bellows. All of it is real chemistry, worked out by careful observation.
visual_style: A whiteboard clay pot with rising bubbles and a zoom into yeast cells turning sugar into ethanol and gas, then a calabash of amasi, then a clay furnace with bellows.
pacing: A slow build in the pot, then a brisk run through amasi and iron.
